title: Binary Search Tree Iterator II
statement:
Build a class `BSTIterator` that walks back and forth over the values of a binary search tree in sorted (in-order) order. Picture the sorted values in a row with a cursor that starts just **before** the first value, so it points at no value yet.

- `BSTIterator(root)` receives the root `TreeNode` (with `val`, `left` and `right`) and places the cursor before the smallest value.
- `hasNext()` returns `true` when some value lies to the right of the cursor, and `false` otherwise.
- `next()` moves the cursor one value to the right and returns the value it now points at. The first call therefore returns the smallest value.
- `hasPrev()` returns `true` when some value lies to the left of the cursor's current value, and `false` otherwise (so it is `false` before the first `next()` and while the cursor is on the smallest value).
- `prev()` moves the cursor one value to the left and returns the value it now points at.

Every call to `next()` or `prev()` is guaranteed to have a value to move to.
constraints: The tree is a valid binary search tree (all values distinct)
At most 10^5 calls in total to hasNext, next, hasPrev and prev
next and prev are only called when a value exists in that direction
notes:
## Intuition

The simple way copies the whole in-order sequence into an array in the constructor; then every call is index arithmetic. That costs O(n) up front even if only a few values are ever read. Instead, produce values lazily, like the classic one-way BST iterator: a stack holds the path of nodes still waiting to be visited, and each `next()` pops one of them. To move backwards we also keep every value produced so far in a list, so `prev()` and repeated `next()` calls over ground already covered just move an index.

## Approach

1. In the constructor, start with an empty `stack`, an empty `values` list and `index = -1` (the cursor before the first value). Push `root` and its chain of left children.
2. `hasNext()`: a next value exists if `values` already holds one after `index`, or the stack still has unvisited nodes.
3. `next()`: increase `index`. If it now points just past the end of `values`, pop the next node in sorted order, push its right child's left chain, and append its value. Return `values[index]`.
4. `hasPrev()`: a previous value exists when `index > 0`.
5. `prev()`: decrease `index` and return `values[index]`.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree is `7` with left child `3` and right child `15` (children `9` and `20`). The constructor pushes `7` and `3`. The first `next()` pops `3` and returns it; the second pops `7`, pushes `15` and `9`, and returns `7`. `prev()` moves `index` back to `0` and returns `3`; the next `next()` returns the stored `7` without touching the stack. `hasNext()` is `true` because the stack is not empty. Three more `next()` calls pop `9`, `15` and `20`. Now `hasNext()` is `false`, `hasPrev()` is `true`, and two `prev()` calls return `15` and `9`.

## Complexity

- Time: `next()` is O(1) amortized, since every node is pushed and popped once (a single call can take O(h)); the other three methods are O(1).
- Space: O(h) for the stack plus O(k) for the `k` values produced so far, at most O(n).

## Pitfalls

- `hasNext()` must also look at the stored `values`: after some `prev()` calls the stack may be empty while stored values still lie ahead.
- Only take a node from the stack when `index` moves past the stored values; otherwise you would skip values after going back.
- `hasPrev()` is about values before the *current* one, so it is `false` while `index` is `0`, not only while it is `-1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | nodes whose value and right subtree are still unvisited |
| `values` | the sorted values produced so far |
| `index` | the cursor: position in `values` of the current value, `-1` before the first |
| `node` | the node being pushed or popped |
